about.title: About
about.lead: Mathematical Formulas is a multi-subject catalog for studying and looking things up carefully, in several languages.
about.missionBody: We want finding a formula to be fast and understanding it to be possible: clear copy, well-rendered LaTeX, and—when it helps—a graphic that teaches the idea.
about.whatBody: Today the site covers Differential Calculus, Calculus II, Basic Physics, and Algebra for engineering and computer science. Each subject has a section index, search, and formula pages.
about.audienceBody: Built for students and teachers who need a stable reference: review, compare notation, or recall an identity without hunting through scattered PDFs.
about.openBody: Content is curated by subject and served by API. We keep improving visualizations and guide clarity based on real classroom and study use.
about.howBody: The catalog is organized by subject and served from an API. Cards combine statements, LaTeX and, when the source includes one, an interactive resource. We do not publish individual authorship or review dates unless the content itself provides them.
about.correctionsBody: If you find a mathematical error, an incomplete translation, or a problem in an interactive resource, use the Contact page and include the subject, formula code, and language.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.lead: How we handle data when you use the site.
privacy.s1Body: The «Mathematical Formulas» site is operated by the project team. For privacy requests, use the Contact page.
privacy.s2Body: No account is required to browse the catalog. We may store local preferences (language and theme) in your browser via cookies or local storage. If you email us, we process the message content and your address to reply. If you submit a review, we store the name you give (optional), the rating, and the comment so we can moderate them and, if approved, show them on the site.
privacy.s3Body: We record page visits in aggregate (path, subject or section when relevant) to improve content. That telemetry is not used to identify people, and the client analytics payload does not send your IP address.
privacy.s4Body: Data is used to provide the service, remember language/theme, answer contact messages, publish approved reviews, and understand which parts of the catalog are used most.
privacy.s5Body: Preferences live on your device until you clear them. Contact messages are kept as long as needed to handle them. Hosting and content storage may involve infrastructure providers under their own terms.
privacy.s6Body: You may request access, correction, or deletion of personal data you sent us (for example a contact email). You can also clear cookies and local storage in your browser.

vizDomain.idea: The domain is the set of x-values for which the function is defined: Dom(f)={x∈ℝ : f(x) is defined}.
vizDomain.ideaNote: Connect the expression, the graph, and the allowed values on the x-axis. The domain line (below) shows valid inputs only, not the graph y=f(x).
vizDomain.rationalHint: In f(x)=1/(x−b), x=b makes the denominator zero. That value is therefore excluded from the domain.
vizDomain.openExcluded: Open circle at x={b}: excluded value (vertical asymptote on the graph).
vizDomain.closedIncluded: Closed endpoint at x={b}: the domain includes this endpoint.
vizDomain.logOpen: Open circle at x={b}: ln(x−b) requires x>{b}.
vizDomain.hintMoveB: Move b and watch the excluded value, the asymptote, and the domain shift together.
vizDomain.hintChangeKind: Change the function type and compare how the condition and the domain change.

vizRiemann.idea: The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums as n → ∞.
vizRiemann.ideaNote: Move the n control and watch the rectangles fill the area more accurately. Change the sum type to see how the sample point affects the error.
vizRiemann.errorShrinks: As n increases, the error decreases toward 0.
vizRiemann.graphAria: Riemann sum of f on [a, b]

polar.idea: In polar coordinates each point is (r, θ): distance from the origin and angle from the polar axis. The 3-petal rose is r = cos(3θ); the 4-petal rose is r = cos(2θ).
polar.note: The full curve is shown in grey; the orange stroke follows θ. Negative r is drawn in the opposite direction.

direction.idea: The formula dy/dx = g(x)h(y) is the slope of the solution at each point. The field draws that slope; click the plane to trace the curve through that point.
direction.note: You can trace up to 5 solutions. Try y(1−y): they all converge to y = 1.
direction.click: Click to trace a particular solution

work.idea: If F is constant, W = F·d. If it varies, W = ∫ F(x) dx: the area under the curve is the accumulated work.

population.idea: The exponential grows or decays without bound. The logistic model levels off at capacity K: every solution tends to K.

trig.idea: Trigonometric substitution removes the radical with Pythagorean identities. The reference triangle converts back to x.
trig.note: Pick a radical and move θ: the sides and the simplification update together.

solids.idea: Rotating the region under f(x) about the x-axis, each point traces a circle. The stack of disks is the solid; its volume is V = π ∫ [f(x)]² dx.
solids.note: Move the angle slider to see the solid form by rotation. Increase n disks for a finer view.

arc.idea: Arc length is approximated by n segments of length √(Δx²+Δy²). The limit is ∫ √(1+[f′(x)]²) dx.

paramTangent.idea: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). If dy/dt = 0 the tangent is horizontal; if dx/dt = 0, vertical.

taylor.idea: The Taylor polynomial Pₙ(x) is the best polynomial approximation of f near x = a. Each extra term reduces the error.
taylor.note: Move n and watch the orange polynomial hug the blue curve. The green band is where the error is < 0.05.
taylor.radiusWarn: Radius of convergence R = {R}. For |x − {center}| ≥ {R} the series diverges regardless of n.

tfc.idea: FTC Part I: If G(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt, then G′(x) = f(x).
tfc.note: Move the x slider. The shaded area in the top panel grows or shrinks with G(x). The slope of the tangent to G (bottom panel) always equals f(x).
tfc.accumUntil: f(t) — accumulated area up to x = {x}

signed.idea: The definite integral measures signed area: regions below the x-axis subtract. Two equal opposite regions cancel even if the geometric area is positive.
signed.note: Try sin(x) from 0 to 2π: the integral is 0 and the geometric area is 4. Then shrink the interval to [0, π].

subst.idea: The substitution u = g(x) simplifies the integrand. The limits change too: from [a, b] in x to [g(a), g(b)] in u. The shaded area is the same.

parts.idea: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du: the rectangle with sides u and v splits into the region under the curve (∫ v du) and the one on the left (∫ u dv).

area.idea: The area between curves is ∫ (upper − lower). If they cross, split the interval at the zeros of f − g.
area.note: For x³ and x, ∫(x³−x) dx on [−1,1] is 0; the geometric area is not.

improper.idea: ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx is defined as lim_'{b→∞'} ∫₁ᵇ f. If the area settles, it converges; if it grows without bound, it diverges.
improper.note: For 1/xᵖ: p > 1 converges to 1/(p−1). The curve 1/x flattens, but its accumulated area keeps growing.

paramCurve.idea: On a parametric curve, x and y depend on a parameter t. The xy-plane does not show t; the side graphs do.
paramCurve.note: On the cycloid the point rolls like a point on a wheel. On Lissajous curves, the frequency ratio sets the lobes.

polarArea.idea: An infinitesimal polar sector has area ½ r² dθ. The integral ½ ∫ r(θ)² dθ adds those sectors.
polarArea.twoCurves: Area between two curves (r and r=1)

series.idea: A series converges if the partial sums Sₙ approach a fixed value. aₙ → 0 is necessary but not sufficient.
series.note: Compare the harmonic series with 1/n²: both terms go to 0, but only the second converges.

numeric.idea: The trapezoid rule uses straight segments (error O(h²)); Simpson uses parabolas (error O(h⁴)) and converges much faster.

tree.idea: There is no universal technique: what matters is recognizing the form of the integrand. The tree follows the questions one asks while integrating.
tree.note: Practice with ∫ x² eˣ dx: what would you answer at each step?
tree.leaves: Leaves: direct formula §2.2 · substitution §4 · parts §5 · trig §6 · trig sub. §7 · partial fractions §8 · numerical §11
tree.arrived: You reached a technique. Reset for another integrand.
tree.qUsub: Is there u = g(x) with g′(x) visible?
tree.qProduct: Is it a product of two different types?
tree.qTrig: Does it contain powers of sin/cos?
tree.qRational: Is it a rational polynomial fraction?
tree.formNumeric: Trapezoid or Simpson if there is no elementary antiderivative

antideriv.idea: F is an antiderivative of f if F′(x) = f(x). The slope of the tangent to F matches the value of f at the same point.

average.idea: The average value is the height of the rectangle with the same area as the region under f. The MVT for integrals guarantees a point c with f(c) = f_avg.
average.areaEq: Area under f = area of the rectangle

shell.idea: Each vertical strip wraps into a cylindrical shell of volume 2π · radius · height · thickness. The integral adds all the shells.

seq.idea: aₙ → L means: for every ε > 0 there is N such that if n > N then |aₙ − L| < ε. The green band is the ε-neighborhood.
seq.inBand: from n = {n} all terms lie in the ε-neighborhood (in the sample)

intTest.idea: If f is continuous, positive and decreasing, rectangles of height f(n) bound the integral. Σ aₙ and ∫ f converge or diverge together.

radius.idea: A power series converges on an interval of radius R centered at a. Outside it, the partial sums diverge.

separable.idea: In a separable ODE, x and y move to opposite sides and are integrated. Solutions form a family parameterized by C.

limit.secantIdea: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient: as h → 0, the secant (orange) approaches the tangent.
limit.notableIdea: Values of sin(x)/x as x → 0: the table and graph show convergence to 1.
limit.note: Move h toward 0 to see how the secant slope approximates the derivative.
limit.informalIdea: As x approaches a, the values f(x) approach L even if f(a) is undefined or different.
limit.epsilonDeltaIdea: For every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0: if 0 < |x−a| < δ, then |f(x)−L| < ε. Adjust ε and δ to see the bands.
limit.epsilonDeltaOk: With this δ, values of f on (a−δ, a+δ) stay inside (L−ε, L+ε).
limit.epsilonDeltaFail: Widen δ or shrink ε: some points in the neighborhood leave the horizontal band.
limit.lateralIdea: The two-sided limit exists only when the left-hand and right-hand limits agree.
limit.eDefinitionIdea: The expression (1+x)^(1/x) approaches e as x → 0 (values on both sides of zero illustrate the two-sided limit).

tangent.idea: The tangent line at x = a has slope f′(a) and passes through (a, f(a)).
tangent.normalIdea: The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent at (a, f(a)); its slope is −1/f′(a).
tangent.horizontalTangent: The tangent is horizontal (f′(a)=0): the normal is vertical and is not drawn in this panel.

kinematics.idea: Velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
kinematics.ideaVelocity: Instantaneous velocity v(t) is the derivative of position s(t): the slope of s at each instant.
kinematics.ideaAccel: Acceleration a(t) is the second derivative of s(t): the derivative of velocity.
kinematics.note: The vertical line marks the selected time t. On s(t), the dashed line has slope v(t).

continuity.definitionIdea: f is continuous at a when lim_'{x→a'} f(x) = f(a): the limit matches the function value.
continuity.discontinuityIdea: Compare three types: removable hole, jump, and vertical asymptote (infinite discontinuity).
continuity.typeRemovable: Removable discontinuity: the limit exists but f(a) does not match (or is undefined).
continuity.typeJump: Jump discontinuity: one-sided limits exist but differ.
continuity.typeInfinite: Infinite discontinuity: the limit diverges (vertical asymptote).

intermediateValue.idea: If f is continuous on [a, b], every value k between f(a) and f(b) is attained at some c ∈ (a, b).
intermediateValue.note: Move k between f(a) and f(b): there is always at least one c with f(c) = k.

productRule.idea: The derivative of a product splits into two terms: f′ times g, plus f times g′.
productRule.match: f′g + fg′ matches the numerical derivative of fg.
productRule.note: Adjust x to see the split at each point.

chainRule.idea: For a composition f(g(x)), the outer rate of change multiplies the inner function's rate.
chainRule.note: The diagram shows the flow x → g(x) → f(g(x)).

logDiff.idea: For y = f(x)^g(x), take ln on both sides first; then differentiate implicitly and solve for y′.
logDiff.match: The logarithmic formula matches the numerical derivative.
logDiff.note: Requires f(x) > 0 at the chosen point.

meanValueTheorem.rolleIdea: If f(a)=f(b), there is an interior c where the tangent is horizontal: f′(c)=0.
meanValueTheorem.mvtIdea: There is a c where the tangent is parallel to the secant through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)).
meanValueTheorem.note: Green is the tangent at c; dashed blue is the secant (MVT only).

concavity.idea: f′ shows growth; f″ shows concavity. Color bands summarize the sign on each interval.
concavity.concaveUpInterval: Concave up: f″ > 0 on the interval
concavity.concaveDownInterval: Concave down: f″ < 0 on the interval

optimization.rectangleIdea: With fixed perimeter P (2x+2y=P), area A(x)=x(P/2−x) is maximized when the rectangle is a square.
optimization.cylinderIdea: With fixed surface area, volume V(r)=Cr/2−πr³ peaks at an optimal radius.

linearApprox.idea: The line L(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a) approximates f near a; error is f(x)−L(x).
linearApprox.note: Orange: linear approximation; green: point on f.

lhopital.idea: For 0/0 or ∞/∞, the quotients f/g and f′/g′ tend to the same limit when hypotheses hold.
lhopital.note: Watch f′/g′ stabilize before f/g as x approaches 0.

implicit.idea: On the circle x²+y²=r², the tangent slope is dy/dx=−x/y.

relatedRates.idea: If volume changes at rate dV/dt, the radius changes as dr/dt=dV/dt÷(4πr²).

asymptote.idea: A rational graph approaches vertical and oblique asymptotes at infinity.

tree.idea: There is no universal technique: recognize the signal in the expression. The tree mirrors the §16 guide questions.
tree.note: Try y = x^x: what would you answer at each step?
tree.leaves: Leaves: L'Hôpital §12 · product/quotient/chain §5 · implicit §13 · log diff §5 · optimization §9 · linearization §10 · power §5
tree.arrived: You reached a technique. Reset for another expression.
tree.qRoot: Is it an indeterminate limit (0/0 or ∞/∞)?
tree.qProduct: Is it a product of two functions?
tree.qImplicit: Is it an implicit equation F(x,y)=0?
tree.qLog: Does it have a variable exponent f(x)^g(x)?
tree.qOptimize: Must you optimize on an interval [a,b]?
tree.qApprox: Must you approximate f near a point a?

ele020.qNote: with fixed Q, increasing C lowers V and U
ele020.vNote: with fixed V, increasing C raises Q and U

guia.prompt: What does the problem statement mention?
guia.pickTopic: Pick a block: motion, forces, conservation, rotation, fluids, waves, heat, or circuits.
guia.pickSection: Pick the section that best matches the statement.
guia.textHelp: Current path and candidate formulas. Use arrows and Enter to navigate; Escape to go back; Home to reset.

voltage_divider.idea: Vo is the fraction R2/(R1+R2) of Vi; a load across R2 lowers that fraction.
voltage_divider.tryIt: Raise R2: Vo approaches Vi. Make RL small: Vo drops.
voltage_divider.caption: Unloaded, Vo = Vi R2/(R1+R2).
voltage_divider.statusI: I1 = {i1} mA · I2 = {i2} mA · IT = {it} mA

unloaded.idea: Unloaded, Vo is exactly Vi R2/(R1+R2).
unloaded.tryIt: Change R1 and R2 and check Vo/Vi = R2/(R1+R2).
unloaded.caption: Unloaded, Vo = Vi R2/(R1+R2).

loaded.idea: RL in parallel with R2 reduces the fraction and therefore Vo.
loaded.tryIt: Lower RL and watch Vo leave the open-circuit value.
loaded.caption: RL in parallel with R2 lowers Vo.

current.idea: The smaller resistor carries more current: I1 = IT R2/(R1+R2).
current.tryIt: Raise R2: more current goes through R1. I1+I2 must equal IT.
current.caption: I1 = IT R2/(R1+R2). The smaller R carries more current.

thevenin_norton.idea: Everything left of the terminals is replaced by VTh (or IN) and RTh = RN.
thevenin_norton.tryIt: Change RL: Vo still divides with RTh. Check VTh = IN RN.
thevenin_norton.caption: The network is replaced by VTh in series with RTh (or IN in parallel with RN = RTh).
thevenin_norton.status: VL = {vl} V · IL = {il} mA · P = {p} mW (Pmax {pmax} mW)

rc_transient.idea: vC (or iL) interpolates the continuous initial value and the settled value with time constant τ.
rc_transient.tryIt: At t = τ the gap to the settled value is 37 %. By 5τ it has essentially settled.
rc_transient.caption: The exponential crosses 63 % or 37 % at t = τ and settles toward 5τ.

rlc_damping.idea: ζ sets the shape: two exponentials, the critical boundary, or a decaying oscillation.
rlc_damping.tryIt: Lower series R: ζ drops and oscillations appear. At critical damping there is no overshoot.
rlc_damping.caption: ζ>1 two exponentials; ζ=1 boundary; ζ<1 decaying oscillation.

phasor_diagram.idea: The RMS phasor rotates at ω; its horizontal projection is the instantaneous sinusoid.
phasor_diagram.tryIt: Change φ: the phasor leads or lags. Compare Vp with Vrms = Vp/√2.
phasor_diagram.caption: The RMS phasor rotates; its projection is the instantaneous sinusoid.

impedance_triangle.idea: Z = R + jX is a triangle: the hypotenuse is |Z| and the angle is arg(Z).
impedance_triangle.tryIt: Set X = 0: the angle vanishes. Flip the sign of X to switch inductive/capacitive.
impedance_triangle.caption: Z = R + jX. |Z| is the hypotenuse.

z.idea: Z = R + jX. |Z| is the hypotenuse and the angle is arg(Z).
z.tryIt: Sweep X from capacitive to inductive and watch the angle sign.
z.caption: Z = R + jX. |Z| is the hypotenuse.

y.idea: Y = 1/Z: magnitude inverts and the angle flips sign. G and B are the legs.
y.tryIt: Raise |Z| and check that |Y| falls. arg(Y) must be −arg(Z).
y.caption: Y = 1/Z. |Y| = 1/|Z| and arg(Y) = −arg(Z).

power.idea: P, Q and S form the power triangle; the angle matches the impedance.
power.tryIt: Zero Q: S equals P. The sign of Q follows X.
power.caption: S² = P² + Q². The angle is that of the impedance.

resonance_curve.idea: At series resonance |Z| is minimum (R); at parallel resonance it is maximum.
resonance_curve.tryIt: Sweep ω around ω0: the curve narrows as Q rises.
resonance_curve.caption: |Z| extreme at ω0.

series.idea: At series resonance X_L + X_C = 0 (X_L = |X_C|) and |Z| is minimum (equal to R).
series.tryIt: Lower R: the valley at ω0 gets deeper and narrower.
series.caption: |Z| minimum at ω0 (series).

parallel.tryIt: Raise R: the |Z| peak at ω0 grows. Away from ω0, |Z| drops.
parallel.caption: |Z| maximum at ω0 (parallel).

bode_filter.idea: |H| passes the useful band; a low-pass falls 20 dB/dec after fc (−3 dB).
bode_filter.tryIt: Change R or C (or L): fc moves. At fc the magnitude should sit near −3 dB.
bode_filter.caption: At fc the gain is −3 dB.

lp_rc.idea: The RC low-pass passes DC and falls 20 dB/dec above fc.
lp_rc.tryIt: Raise C: fc drops. At fc, |H| should be −3 dB.
lp_rc.caption: At fc the gain is −3 dB. Above fc, |H| falls 20 dB/dec.

fc.idea: fc = 1/(2π RC) is the −3 dB point of a first-order Bode plot.
fc.caption: fc = 1/(2π RC) marks the −3 dB point.

hp_rc.idea: The RC high-pass rises +20 dB/dec below fc and approaches 0 dB above cutoff.
hp_rc.tryIt: Look left of fc: |H| rises, it does not fall. Above fc it flattens.
hp_rc.caption: Below fc, |H| rises +20 dB/dec; above fc it approaches 0 dB.

lp_rl.idea: The RL low-pass has cutoff fc = R/(2π L) and falls 20 dB/dec above fc.
lp_rl.tryIt: Raise L: fc drops. The controls are R and L, not a capacitor.
lp_rl.caption: Cutoff fc = R/(2π L). Above fc, |H| falls 20 dB/dec.

diode_iv.idea: The diode barely conducts below threshold and then fires forward; the rectifier clips or folds the sinusoid.
diode_iv.tryIt: On the IV curve, cross ~0.7 V. For half-wave compare Vavg = Vp/π with the positive clip.
diode_iv.caption: IV: strong conduction past threshold. Rectifier: clips or folds the sinusoid.

bjt_load_line.idea: The load line joins (VCE=VCC, IC=0) to (VCE=0, IC=VCC/RC); Q runs through cutoff, active and saturation.
bjt_load_line.tryIt: IB = 0: cutoff. Raise IB until VCE sticks at ~0.2 V: saturation, IC is no longer β IB.
bjt_load_line.caption: The load line joins (VCE=VCC, IC=0) to (VCE=0, IC=VCC/RC). Q traverses the regions.

opamp_circuit.idea: With negative feedback v+ ≈ v− (virtual node) and the resistors set Av.
opamp_circuit.tryIt: Inverter Av = −Rf/Rg. Follower Av = 1. If |Av Vin| exceeds Vsat, the output flattens.
opamp_circuit.caption: With negative feedback, v+ ≈ v− (virtual node).

inv.idea: The inverter uses the virtual node: Vo = −(Rf/Rin) Vin.
inv.tryIt: Raise Rf: |Av| grows. Vo has the opposite sign of Vin.
inv.caption: Inverter: Vo = −(Rf/Rg) Vin with virtual ground.

ninv.idea: The non-inverter has gain 1+Rf/Rg with the input on v+.
ninv.tryIt: Set Rf = Rg: Av = 2. Vin and Vo have the same sign.
ninv.caption: Non-inverting: Av = 1+Rf/Rg.

buffer.idea: The follower is a non-inverter of gain 1: Vo = Vin.
buffer.tryIt: Change Vin: Vo copies it within ±Vsat.
buffer.caption: Follower: gain 1.

int.idea: The integrator has C in the feedback: Vo = −(1/RC) ∫ Vin dt, a ramp if Vin is constant.
int.tryIt: Raise C or R: the RC constant grows and the ramp slows.
int.caption: Integrator: capacitor in the loop, RC constant and output ramp.

cmos_vtc.idea: The CMOS VTC inverts: low Vin gives VOH, high Vin gives VOL, and VIH/VIL set NMH and NML.
cmos_vtc.tryIt: Move Vin across VIL and VIH: the margins are VOH−VIH and VIL−VOL, not the rails alone.
cmos_vtc.caption: The CMOS VTC inverts: low Vin gives VOH; high Vin gives VOL. Thresholds set NMH and NML.
cmos_vtc.status: Vo = {vo} V · NMH = {nmh} V · NML = {nml} V

flip_flop_timing.idea: D must sit still tsu before the edge and th after; otherwise metastability.
flip_flop_timing.tryIt: Widen tsu: the critical window grows. The edge is the only instant that copies D to Q.
flip_flop_timing.caption: D must be stable tsu before the edge and th after. Otherwise metastability.

sampling_pwm.idea: fs > 2 fmax avoids aliasing; n bits split VFS into 2^n levels; PWM uses ton/T.
sampling_pwm.tryIt: Drop fs below 2 fmax: aliasing appears. In PWM, duty 0.5 leaves the pulse at mid-period.
sampling_pwm.caption: Nyquist, quantization or PWM according to the mode.

nyquist.tryIt: Drop fs below 2 fmax and read the aliasing warning.
nyquist.caption: Nyquist: fs > 2 fmax.

quant.idea: n bits split VFS into 2^n levels; the step is Δ = VFS/2^n.
quant.tryIt: Raise bits: Δ shrinks and there are more steps.
quant.caption: Quantization splits VFS into 2^n levels.

pwm.idea: PWM duty is ton/T, the high fraction of the period.
pwm.tryIt: Move duty: the high pulse occupies that fraction of the period.
pwm.caption: PWM: duty is ton/T.

r2r.idea: The R-2R DAC sums binary weights: Vo = −Vref Σ bk/2^k through the R and 2R network.
r2r.tryIt: Change the code: each 1-bit contributes Vref/2, Vref/4, … This is not a Δ quantizer.
r2r.caption: R-2R ladder: binary weights and DAC voltage Vo = −Vref Σ bk/2^k.

electronics_guide.idea: The signal in the statement (DC, transient, sinusoid, device or digital) points to a block, not to memorizing 188 IDs.
electronics_guide.tryIt: Pick «RC transient»: the tree ends at τ, v(0+) and v(∞). For a flip-flop, look at setup and hold.
electronics_guide.caption: Choose the signal in the statement: DC, transient, sinusoid, device or digital.
electronics_guide.waiting: Choose a signal to see the matching branch.

results.dc: Reduce the resistive network and find the Thévenin or Norton equivalent: Vth, Rth and In.
results.transient: For an RC, the tree ends at τ = RC, v(0+) and v(∞). For an RL, at τ = L/R, i(0+) and i(∞).
results.rlc: Write the characteristic equation and classify ζ: overdamped, critical or underdamped.
results.phasors: Convert to RMS phasors and impedances.
results.filter: Find H(jω), the cutoffs, the slope and the load effect.
results.diode: Choose the diode model, identify conduction and estimate the ripple.
results.opamp: Confirm the feedback, the linear region and the saturation limit.
results.ff: Check the clock, setup, hold and the next state.
